description: GEO services — getting your business cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. Structured data, answer-shaped content and AI crawler access.
sections:
Home Generative Engine Optimization
S Service
  • Discipline AI search visibility
  • Targets ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini
  • Status Early, and uncrowded

GEO is the work of becoming the source AI assistants cite.

Start a project See the work

01 The search

The search box is moving

A growing share of questions that used to produce ten blue links now produce a written answer with a handful of citations.

02 What GEO

What GEO work involves

Structured data

01

Schema.org markup describing the business, its services, its location and its reviews as machine-readable facts rather than prose an assistant has to infer from.

Answer-shaped content

02

Direct answers placed high on the page, in the 40-to-60 word block an assistant can lift whole.

Crawler access

03

GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended and the rest explicitly permitted in robots.txt.

Server-rendered content

04

AI crawlers largely do not execute JavaScript.

llms.txt

05

A plain-language summary written for machines, giving an assistant a clean account of who you are and what you do.

Entity consistency

06

The same name, address, phone and description everywhere, so an assistant can be confident two mentions are the same business.

03 Why it

Why it is worth doing now

SEO is thirty years old and every competitive term has someone defending it.

04 Questions

Questions people actually ask

01 What is Generative Engine Optimization?

GEO is optimising a site so that AI assistants — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and others — cite it as a source when answering questions.

02 Is GEO different from SEO?

It builds on SEO and adds to it. Fast, crawlable, well-structured pages help both.

03 How do I get cited by ChatGPT?

Allow OpenAI's crawlers in robots.txt, publish content that answers real questions directly and early, mark the facts up in schema so they can be attributed, and make sure the content exists in the HTML rather than appearing after JavaScript runs.

Redesign is usually the wrong first question

02 What the

What the diagnosis looks at

Indexing, canonicals, redirects, structured data, and whether the site is even eligible to rank.

Whether a first-time visitor can find what they came for without guessing.

Conversion path

05

Whether it is obvious what to do next, and whether the mechanism for doing it actually works.

Content

03 Two ways

Two ways it goes

Sometimes the diagnosis says the foundation is sound and three specific things are wrong.

04 Questions

Questions people actually ask

01 How do I know if I need a redesign or just fixes?

Look at the diagnosis before deciding. If the site loads reasonably, is indexed, and works on a phone, targeted fixes will usually get you most of the way.

02 Will I lose my Google rankings if I redesign?

Only if the migration is done carelessly. Rankings are lost when URLs change without redirects, when content is cut, or when the new site blocks crawling.

03 Can you redesign without changing our branding?

Yes. Plenty of redesigns keep the identity entirely and change only the things that were costing money.

S Service

Speed work measured the way visitors experience it: a mid-range Android phone on mobile data, not a desktop test on office broadband.

Start a project See the work

01 The score

The score is not the point

A perfect score from a testing tool run on a fast desktop connection tells you very little about the person trying to load your site on a bus.

02 Where the

Where the time usually goes

Images

01

Almost always the largest cost. Uncompressed, wrongly sized, in outdated formats, and loaded before anything the visitor can see.

JavaScript

02

Frameworks and plugins loaded for features a page never uses.

Render-blocking resources

03

Stylesheets and scripts in the head that stop the page painting until they arrive.

Fonts

04

Custom fonts that block text from appearing, or swap in late and shift the layout under the reader.

Third-party tags

05

Analytics, chat widgets, pixels and embeds, each adding a connection to somewhere you do not control.

Server response

06

Slow hosting or an uncached backend that delays the very first byte, before the browser can start on anything else.

03 What Core

What Core Web Vitals actually measure

LCP — Largest Contentful Paint

01

How long until the main thing appears. Usually an image or headline.

INP — Interaction to Next Paint

02

How quickly the page responds when someone taps.

CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift

03

How much the page moves while loading. The reason you tap the wrong thing on a news site.

04 Questions

Questions people actually ask

01 Why is my website slow?

Most often images that are far larger than the space they are shown in, followed by JavaScript the page does not need.

02 Does site speed affect Google rankings?

Yes, though less dramatically than often claimed.

03 What is a good Core Web Vitals score?

LCP under 2.5 seconds, INP under 200 milliseconds, CLS under 0.1 — measured on real mobile visits, not a lab test.
